rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Point charges repel or attract with k |q1 q2| / r^2 along the line joining them. The two forces are equal and opposite. Several charges are handled by adding force vectors, and a charge inside a uniform spherical shell feels no net force from that shell.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Coulomb's law gives the force between two point charges: F = k |q1 q2| / r^2, with k = 9.0 × 10^9 in SI units. The force is along the line joining the charges. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.  ·  Doubling either charge doubles the force. Doubling the distance divides the force by four. The force on each charge has the same magnitude even when the charges are unequal.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Inverse square.  ·  Like charges repel.  ·  The two forces are equal and opposite.  ·  Superposition uses components.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Coulomb: F = (1/4πε₀)·q₁q₂/r². Electric field E = F/q = kq/r²; for a line/dipole use superposition.  ·  Gauss's law: ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε₀ — powerful for spherical/cylindrical/planar symmetry.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Doubling the separation multiplies F by → C  ·  Like charges → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: A third charge feels the vector sum of the forces from the other two. If the charges are not on one line, resolve each force into components before adding.  ·  In a uniform insulating medium the force is the vacuum force divided by the dielectric constant. The medium does not cancel the law. It reduces the force.  ·  Spherical charge distributions, outside the sphere, act as if their charge were at the centre. Inside a uniform spherical shell the field is zero, so a charge there feels no net force from the shell.
